Trump Dumped Micron, Up 338% in a Year. The Memory Cycle Decides Who's Right ©Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok and Adam Smigielski from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

President Trump's brokerage accounts sold $251,000 to $515,000 of Micron stock in August, plus $1 million to $5 million of AMD, and bought as much as $25.3 million of Meta Platforms.

Outside managers run those accounts, but selling Micron is still a bet that the memory shortage behind its run is near its peak.

Micron's gross margin went from 2.7% in fiscal 2023 to 80.7% in fiscal 2026, which shows how much its profits depend on memory prices.

Analysts expect normalized EPS to more than double to $176.55 in fiscal 2027, so the numbers say the sale came early, and Micron's next report is the test.

Micron Technology (MU:NASDAQ) is up 338% in a year, and a new disclosure shows President Trump's portfolio heading for the exit.

His accounts sold Micron in August, sold Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) that month too, and made their biggest purchase in Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ).

What exactly happened

Trump's newest filing with the Office of Government Ethics lists 517 trades. Three of them stand out:

Micron: net sales of $251,000 to $515,000

AMD: a sale of $1 million to $5 million

Meta: net purchases of $5.1 million to $25.3 million, the month's largest buy

Third-party firms manage these accounts, so Trump didn't make the call himself. And next to the Meta purchase, the Micron sale is small potatoes.

But it's the most interesting one to me for the very simple reason that…whoever sold made a real bet on the memory cycle. After a 338% year, every Micron holder is making that same bet, one way or the other.

Margins show where the cycle stands

Memory is a commodity. As Morningstar analyst William Kerwin wrote, "We view DRAM and NAND as commodity-like products prone to market supply/demand dynamics and steady pricing erosion."

You can see it in Micron's gross margin. It fell to 2.7% in fiscal 2023, then climbed to 80.7% in fiscal 2026 as AI demand ran into a memory shortage…

Micron Technology (MU): gross margin (%), fiscal 2022–2026 (years to August) (TIKR)

That's far above the 45.2% from fiscal 2022. (And I mean, fiscal 2023 hardly bears mentioning, right?)

The latest quarter shows the shortage at full tilt. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, revenue rose 379% to $54 billion. Adjusted EPS came in at $33.42, up from $3.03 a year earlier.

When the shortage eases, memory prices fall, and Micron's earnings fall with them. Selling now is a bet that day is close.

Analysts don't see a peak yet

Wall Street expects profits to keep climbing for two more years. Consensus has normalized EPS going from $75.52 in fiscal 2026 to $176.55 in fiscal 2027 (35 analysts), and then to $206.89 in fiscal 2028 (36 analysts)…

With a market cap of around $863 billion, many investors believe Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is on track to regain its $1-trillion status after losing it in early October 2026. Wall Street analysts are quite optimistic about the stock, and the high target price of $1,250 is more than double today's closing price.

Screenshot courtesy of www.barchart.com

But how can investors play this beyond a typical buy-and-hold strategy?

Two option strategies let them capitalize on future upside potential. The only difference is whether you're willing to pay up front or prefer to earn at the start of the trade. Let's take a look at both.

How a Deep ITM LEAPS Call Works on AMD

Call options are time-bound contracts that give the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying asset at a set strike price on or before the expiration date. The goal is to benefit from a bullish move in the underlying stock, preferably before the contract expires.

In-the-money (ITM) means an option has real, or intrinsic, value. For call options, this happens when the stock trades above the strike price. If you're holding a 100-strike call on a stock trading at $150, your option is in the money with $50 of intrinsic value. But options also have time or extrinsic value, so that call will likely sell for more than $50.

Now, LEAPS, or Long-Term Equity Anticipation Securities, are standard option contracts that expire in one year or more.

Put together, a deep ITM LEAPS call is a long-term call option with a strike price well below the underlying stock's current market price. It's like renting the stock for a fixed period, say, one to two years, allowing you to participate in much of the upside without paying for the full 100 shares outright. These calls also have less theta (time decay) than call options that expire in weeks or months, which measures how much value an option loses each day simply because time passes.

Deep ITM LEAPS calls typically have a delta of around 0.80 to 0.95. Delta, like theta, is an options Greek. It measures how much an option's price is expected to change for every $1 move in the underlying stock. The higher the delta, the more closely the option's price tracks the stock.

Our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade includes both the chip designer and the foundry. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) offers processor and accelerator upside. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) offers exposure to manufacturing many customers' designs. Their starting cash prices set very different hurdles.

AMD vs. TSMC: How Much Faster Must AMD's Cash Flow Grow?

Photo by Christian Wiediger on Unsplash

The starting multiple matters

At October 16 prices, AMD's $863.17 billion equity value compared with $8.40 billion of trailing operating cash after capital expenditure: roughly 103 times. TSMC's comparable cash figure was $45.53 billion. Applying its $412.61 depositary-share price to 25.93 billion ordinary shares, with five ordinary shares per depositary share, gives a U.S.-price-implied equity value near $2.14 trillion and a multiple near 47.

That depositary-share adjustment matters. Mixing ordinary shares with the U.S. trading price would inflate capitalization fivefold. Even correctly calculated multiples are historical snapshots: investment spending, working capital and currency translation can change the denominator.

AMD's growth opportunity is substantial. Second-quarter data-center revenue reached $6.72 billion, more than double a year earlier. Its challenge is turning broader adoption into cash after engineering and investment costs. Our Nvidia-AMD margin analysis tests how much room AMD currently has for pricing disappointment.

A common ending multiple exposes the hurdle

Suppose TSMC's cash flow grows 10% annually for ten years. At unchanged share prices and share counts, AMD would need about 19% annual growth to reach the same ending cash-flow multiple. The calculation compounds the starting multiple gap over ten years; it does not assume either stock actually delivers those returns.

If TSMC's cash growth is zero, AMD's catch-up hurdle is about 8% annually. If TSMC grows 15%, AMD needs about 24%. These are scenarios, not company guidance or justified growth forecasts. AMD could deserve a different ending multiple, and dilution would make the required company-wide growth higher for a given per-share result.

TSMC also has to earn its cash. New fabrication capacity can consume funds long before it produces revenue, while utilization and geographic disruption can undermine returns.

The investment test

Geography also changes the return investors may require.

Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 164 from 134 for AMD and to 249 from 234 for TSMC. Marshall Wace increased AMD shares 3%, while Fisher increased TSMC shares 2%. The aggregate increases do not imply every manager agreed. AMD's September 30 short interest was 2.42% of float.
